one_liner: Header-only C++ learned ordered index for numeric keys; beats STX B+Tree up to 4x on in-memory lookups and inserts.
what_it_does: ALEX is an in-memory, single-threaded ordered index for numeric keys. Like a B+Tree, it supports point lookups, range scans, inserts, updates and deletes. It ships as headers with three front ends: AlexMap and AlexMultiMap mimic std::map and std::multimap (operator[], at, find, lower_bound/upper_bound, equal_range, erase, forward and reverse iterators), and the lower-level Alex class adds get_payload() and tuning setters such as set_expected_insert_frac() and set_max_node_size(). The recommended way to build one is bulk_load() from a sorted array; the iterator-range constructor copies the input and sorts it first.
how_it_is_fast: ALEX is an updatable Recursive Model Index (RMI). Each internal node holds a linear regression that computes the child slot directly, so no key comparisons happen above the leaves. Leaves are Gapped Arrays filled by model-based inserts, so most keys sit at or near their predicted slot and an exponential search from the prediction finishes in a few steps; a per-leaf bitmap marks gaps, and popcnt/lzcnt/tzcnt find the nearest gap for an insert. Cost models (expected search iterations and key shifts) plus a 'fanout tree' decide the node layout at bulk load and whether a full leaf expands and retrains, splits sideways or splits downward.
when_to_use: Single-threaded (or externally locked) in-memory ordered map with 8-byte integer or double keys and small fixed-size payloads, where point lookups dominate: the paper reports up to 4.1x read-only throughput over a page-size-tuned STX B+Tree.

Read-only to read-intensive mixes with inserts (for example 95% reads / 5% inserts): the independent GRE study found single-core learned indexes such as ALEX beat traditional indexes there regardless of how hard the key distribution is.

Short range scans (up to about 1000 keys) mixed with lookups and inserts: the paper shows up to 2.27x over B+Tree on its 95% scan / 5% insert workload, helped by large leaves (median 161 KB on longitudes).
Append-heavy keys such as timestamps or sequence IDs: leaves detect append-mostly behavior, and the paper shows up to 3.6x over B+Tree when the remaining keys are inserted in ascending order.
Memory-constrained cases where you would otherwise pick LIPP: GRE measured ALEX as the most space-efficient of its three top performers, with LIPP using 4-5x more memory.
when_not_to_use: Concurrent access: the public code has no locking, and even lookups write per-node statistics. GRE's concurrent port (ALEX+, based on the APEX protocol) lives in a research repo (gre4index/GRE) that declares no license.
String, composite or custom-ordered keys: a static_assert requires an arithmetic key type and the default AlexCompare comparator.

Hard, locally nonlinear key distributions with 50% or more writes: GRE found learned indexes lose to traditional indexes there. ALEX's key shifts per insert grow with hardness (42.6 on genome versus 8.1 on covid), and its 99.9th-percentile insert latency is high on osm and genome. The README also warns that extreme outlier keys inflate the key domain and tree depth.

Workloads whose distribution shifts from easy to hard after bulk load (GRE measured up to a 52% throughput drop), large payloads under heavy writes (payloads are stored inline and copied on every expansion or split; ART matched ALEX on write-only YCSB with 80-byte payloads), and long scans past about 1000 keys, where a B+Tree tuned for scans wins.
Non-x86 targets: the code includes x86intrin.h, runs inline cpuid assembly and calls _lzcnt_u64/_tzcnt_u64/_mm_popcnt_u64 unconditionally, so aarch64 (Apple Silicon, Graviton) needs porting.

integration.dependencies: none beyond the C++ standard library and x86 intrinsics headers (doctest is downloaded by CMake only for the unit tests)
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (README and CMakeLists). The shipped CMake uses -O3 -march=native for GCC/Clang and /O2 /arch:AVX2 for MSVC. The CPU and flags must enable POPCNT and LZCNT/TZCNT (BMI, Haswell or later), or builds fail with 'target specific option mismatch' (issues #13, #31). C++20 against libc++ will probably not compile: ALEX uses std::allocator::rebind and destroy, which the libc++ headers declare only for C++17 and earlier (inferred from the headers, not built).
integration.platforms: x86-64 only (Linux, Intel macOS, Windows/MSVC); no aarch64 code path
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe; the README says ALEX runs single-threaded. Lookups (find, get_payload, lower_bound) increment per-node and global counters that feed the cost models, so even concurrent readers race without an external lock.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — AlexMap fills the same ordered-map role as STX B+Tree and std::map and mirrors most of the std::map API. However, keys must be numeric with the default comparator, operator* returns a copy of the pair rather than a reference, and forward iterators cannot be decremented (a separate reverse_iterator exists). Alex::insert does not overwrite an existing key, and iterators and references do not stay stable across inserts.

gotchas: Inserts shift keys inside a leaf, and expansions or splits allocate new slot arrays and free the old ones. Iterators and payload references (from operator[], at() or iterator payload()) can therefore dangle after any insert, unlike std::map. The repo does not document these invalidation rules.

Payload slots are default-constructed with placement new and freed with deallocate(); neither resize nor the leaf destructor calls payload destructors. Use trivially destructible payloads (integers, POD structs, raw pointers); a std::string payload would leak.

Gap slots after a leaf's largest key hold std::numeric_limits<T>::max() as an end sentinel, and find_key compares slot contents without checking the gap bitmap. Treat max() as a reserved key value (inferred from the source, not documented).

bulk_load() expects sorted input and silently does nothing if the index is not empty or num_keys <= 0. Key counts are int, so one index cannot exceed about 2.1 billion keys. The paper's '800x-2000x smaller index' counts inner nodes only; leaves start 70% full, and GRE found that no learned index saves more than 3.2x end to end versus traditional indexes.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick ALEX over LIPP when memory or a path to concurrency matters: GRE measured LIPP at 4-5x ALEX's memory and found LIPP scales poorly when parallelized, while ALEX+ scales well. Pick LIPP or CARMI when raw single-threaded lookup speed is all that counts (their catalog entries claim up to 2.8x and on average 1.9x over ALEX), PGM-index for write-only or static data (GRE saw PGM with the best insert throughput at 100% writes but lookups dominated by ALEX), and ART Synchronized when you need a concurrent index today.
verified_claims_summary: In the SIGMOD'20 paper (single-threaded, Intel Core i9-9900K, 64 GB RAM), ALEX reached up to 4.1x read-only and 4.0x read-write throughput over an STX B+Tree whose page size was grid-searched per dataset and workload, and up to 2.2x over a 2-level RMI Learned Index. The tests used 8-byte keys: 1B longitudes, 200M longlat, 190M lognormal and 200M YCSB keys with 80-byte payloads. The paper names no compiler or flags, does not compare against std::map, and the repo's benchmark runs ALEX alone. GRE (PVLDB'22, gcc 8.3.0 -O3, Xeon Platinum 8268) independently ranked ALEX among the top single-threaded indexes against STX B+Tree, ART and HOT, except on hard data with 50% or more writes.
status_note: Stale: the last commit is 2024-03-12 (bug-fix PR #29), and issues about runaway memory on insert (#30) and unassigned child pointers in expand_root (#26) have no maintainer reply. It is MIT-licensed and six headers, so it is easy to vendor on x86-64 with C++14/17.
